claims.statement: There is no single consensus on whether rational agents should defer to epistemic peers in all cases of disagreement.

support.explanation: The source explicitly identifies the lack of consensus by outlining three distinct theoretical responses to disagreement.
support.passage: In the current debate of the epistemology of peer disagreement, it is controversial whether one is rationally required to suspend one’s judgment when disputing with peers. Three different views have been proposed: (1) The Conciliatory view: we should always move at least a bit in the direction of the epistemic peer’s. (2) The Stubborn view: we should always not be moved by peer disagreement. (3) The Non-Conciliatory view: in some cases of peer disagreement we should be moved by peer disagreement, but in some cases of peer disagreement we should not be moved by peer disagreement.

actions.findings: There is no single consensus on whether rational agents should defer to epistemic peers in all cases of disagreement. [source-8259eb518d4a419c]
actions.limitations: The current evidence is limited to a single thesis overview of philosophical positions. Computational or algorithmic implementations of these positions in AI agents remain unexamined.
actions.next_questions: How do these philosophical positions map to specific consensus-seeking algorithms in multi-agent systems? Are there objective metrics to determine when a 'peer' is actually an epistemic equal?
actions.reason: This notebook synthesizes the initial source material into a structured assessment of the project's core philosophical question.
actions.summary: Epistemic disagreement occurs when agents with identical evidence reach different conclusions. The literature identifies three primary stances: the Conciliatory view, the Stubborn view, and the Non-Conciliatory view. These stances interact with Uniqueness and Permissivism; Uniqueness asserts that evidence dictates one correct rational attitude, whereas Permissivism allows for multiple. Current evidence suggests that unconditional deference (Conciliatory view) may be less tenable than a nuanced approach that accounts for case-specific conditions.
actions.title: Rational Responses to Epistemic Peer Disagreement

proposal.summary: This journal entry synthesizes initial evidence regarding epistemic peer disagreement, contrasting different rational responses to peer dissent and assessing the applicability of Uniqueness and Permissivism theses to intelligent system judgment.
proposal.title: Synthesis: Peer Disagreement and Independent Judgment
